title: Pre-release capability testing displaces the open-weights ban debate by H1 2027
body: Anthropic published its position on open-weights models on Monday, July 27, and the opening move is a denial rather than a demand: Dario Amodei writes that Anthropic has never advocated for a ban, and that open-weights models without dangerous capabilities are a public good that costs nothing beyond the compute to run them. On Tuesday, July 28, Jensen Huang put NVIDIA on the same side of that particular question, posting that open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable national sovereignty, having already signed the open letter alongside IBM, Mozilla, Microsoft and Meta. The two do not agree about much else here — Huang says open models strengthen safety, while Amodei accepts that open weights expand access and competition but disputes that they necessarily improve safety or advantage defenders over attackers — and that is precisely why their agreement on the prohibition matters: the prohibition is no longer where the argument lives. What is left contested is the third of Anthropic's three asks, that every sufficiently capable model, open or closed and regardless of country of origin, be tested for cyber, biological and alignment risk before release. The load-bearing words are 'sufficiently capable'. That is a threshold rather than a principle, and it quietly decides which releases a gate touches, who runs the battery, and whether an origin-neutral rule can reach a foreign open-weight release at all. This prediction says that threshold becomes the contested text: by H1 2027, an explicit capability line paired with a named pre-release test for cyber, biological and alignment risk appears in at least one instrument written to bind — a federal rule or bill text, or a multi-signatory industry specification — and the open-weights side argues about where the line sits and who holds the pen rather than about whether weights may be published at all. The competing line is already on the table, which is why this should be a fight rather than a drafting exercise: the administration is weighing restrictions on Chinese AI labs, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has threatened to sanction Chinese developers of open-weight frontier models, a rule keyed to origin rather than to capability. Anthropic's own concession, that many of the companies running industrial-scale distillation operations also publish open weights, is what makes an origin-keyed or licence-keyed line messy and leaves the capability-keyed one as the residual option. The difficulty of drafting it is visible in the same week's other document: Amodei also signed the Pacing the Frontier statement published Tuesday, July 28, which says the world currently lacks the technical and governance tools to pace frontier-wide progress at all. A pre-release gate that nobody has yet specified is the narrower instance of that same missing toolkit, and specifying it is the work the next three quarters of this argument will be about.

reasoning.because: Anthropic (July 27) and NVIDIA's Jensen Huang (July 28) both rejected a blanket open-weights ban
reasoning.given: Once both camps concede the ban, the only lever left is the line deciding which models get gated
reasoning.so_that: An explicit capability threshold plus a named pre-release cyber, biological and alignment test lands in binding text
reasoning.landing: by H1 2027; threshold text in a US federal instrument or an industry spec
reasoning.plain_language: Both sides now agree open models shouldn't be banned, so the fight moves to which models must be safety-tested first.

summary: Anthropic and NVIDIA landed on the same side of the open-weights ban question within two days, which moves the argument onto the gate instead. Expect the contested text by H1 2027 to be a capability threshold plus a pre-release cyber, biological and alignment test.
